claims.text: The initial Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles are solid, single-phase, and chemically homogeneous.
Different constituents of nanoscale CoCrFeNiCu exhibit different vibrational behavior.
Local differences in atomic vibrational amplitude arise from differences in bonding strength and atomic mass.
Local vibrational-amplitude differences govern heterogeneous premelting in Fe–Ni–Cr–Co–Cu nanoparticles.
Heterogeneous premelting begins through localized disorder before complete melting.
MD can be used to study nanoscale thermophysical and phonon properties of CoCrFeNiCu.
Paired MD and ultrafast electron diffraction can quantify spatially local vibrational amplitudes and atomic-displacement distributions during heating.
Specific atomic sites undergo phonon softening because of local differences in atomic mass and bonding strength.
Atoms having higher vibrational amplitudes because of weaker bonding or heavier mass become unstable at lower temperatures.
The atoms that become unstable at lower temperatures act as nucleation sites for localized disorder and premelting.
Regions without the proposed high-amplitude sites remain intact until higher temperatures.
Relative to a uniform-vibration baseline, the HEA nanoparticles will develop localized regions of increased vibrational disorder before complete melting.
The predicted premelting disorder will produce broader diffraction peaks.
The predicted premelting disorder will be associated with reduced local Debye temperatures.
The hypothesis applies when atomic-scale bonding and mass differences dominate nanoparticle thermal response.
The hypothesis may fail for larger particles when surface effects or unrelated kinetic factors obscure vibrational dynamics.
A lack of detectable spatial vibrational heterogeneity near melting would falsify the proposed differential-thermal-agitation mechanism.
